newsitem.title: UK: Dollar slides amid fears about G3 policy change.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slides amid fears about G3 policy change.

text.p: The dollar racked up losses during the European morning as fears gripped the market that the G3 strong-dollar policy was coming apart at the seams.

The dollar slid overnight after Japanese finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara was quoted as saying the dollar/yen's correction of last year's plunge was about to end and the finance ministry was not trying to weaken the yen further.
The comments shocked a market which had been nervously watching the United States for any post-election retreat from its much-vaunted commitment to a firmer currency.

"The (Sakakibara) remarks highlight the likelihood that the pre-election strong dollar policy was to some extent contrived. The market will now become suspicious that the U.S. attitude towards the strong dollar will be similarly relaxed," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London.
Analysts said the comments carried special resonance as they came from the man dubbed "Mr Yen" for his part in dragging the yen down from last year's post-war high against the dollar.
"The comfortable consensus in G3 policy towards foreign exchange -- get the dollar up -- is unravelling faster than expected," said Klaus Baader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"But the initial signal did not come from the new U.S. administration as many expected but from Japan, where it appears the groundwork is being laid for a rate hike," said Baader, who is a senior currency economist at DMG here.
The dollar was quoted at 111.85/95 yen by 1121 GMT, its weakest since mid-October and far below Wednesday's European close of 113.90/4.00 and intraday high of 114.67.
Dollar/mark fell to 1.5082/86 from yesterday's 1.5178/81, weighed down by mark/yen's fall to 74.12/15 from 75.09/12.
Some analysts said the G3 was not about to reverse policy and Sakakibara had merely wished to cap dollar/yen.
But while the U.S. and Japan may have reasons for wanting a lid on the dollar, Germany has precious little interest in a weaker dollar/mark, analysts said.
A sustained shift to marks could destabilise the whole process of European monetary union and strangle the fragile German export-led recovery.
Germany's economic woes were highlighted by new data showing unemployment there soared a seasonally-adjusted 41,000 from September -- way beyond forecasts of a 10,000 rise.
With extreme fiscal austerity likely in 1997, the prospect of a domestic economic pick-up looks remote, analysts said.
Yesterday's data showing Japan's trade surplus shot up 22.1 percent in the first 20 days of October versus a year earlier may have spurred Sakakibara into speaking out, they said.
"I don't think it signals a change in policy by the Japanese authorities," said DKB International economist Nick Stamenkovic.
"The yen's weakness has been a key part of Japanese policy to allow the economy to recover so the authorities will be very reluctant to see a reversal."
It now remains to be seen whether officials in the new U.S. administration oppose the strong-dollar policy because of its potentially adverse impact on U.S. exports, analysts said.

The weak jobless data were seen igniting some hopes of an eventual cut in the Bundesbank's repo rate. The German central bank left all interest rates on hold, as expected, after today's council meeting.

Also in Germany, finance minister Theo Waigel said moves to weaken the strict fiscal targets for European monetary union would be wrong and that European politicians and finance ministers wanted strict adherence to EMU targets.
The mark was quoted at 1005.50/75 lire and 3.3818/23 French francs by 1157 GMT, up from 1002.50/3.00 and 3.3788/92 in late Europe on Wednesday. -- London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
